utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Milovancevic, can I just -- I'm sorry to do this to you. May I just please warn the witness. Mr. Licina, yesterday before you started your testimony you made an oath, or rather, a declaration to tell the truth, nothing else -- the whole truth and nothing else but the truth. You are still bound by that declaration to tell the truth, nothing else but the truth. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Licina.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Defence will continue with your examination-in-chief. I will ask you once again to think of the interpreters and to speak slowly so that the interpreters can keep up, and to avoid overlapping between my questions and your answers. Thank you. Yesterday, Mr. Licina, you explained that you were a member of the assembly, first of all of the SAO Krajina and then the Republic of Serbian Krajina, throughout its existence. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the assembly of the SAO Krajina and of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and after the elections of 1993, I was a deputy in the assembly of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. That was after 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this period, while you were a deputy, did you hold any positions in the main executive board of the Serb Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I continued to be a member of the main executive board, and I haven't said yet that in the assembly I was a member of parliamentary committees for defence and security and for information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what organs of authority existed on the territory of the SAO Krajina and afterwards the Republic of Serb Krajina. I am bearing in mind the legislative, executive, and judiciary branches, if they existed.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the territory of the SAO Krajina, there were the legislative, executive, and judicial branches of government. There was the assembly, the government, and the courts that existed in the SAO Krajina respectively. After 1991, after the 19th of December, 1991, when the Republic of Serbian Krajina was formed, there were also the legislative, executive, and judicial branches of government. There was the assembly of the Republic of Serbian Krajina which was the legislative branch, then there was the president of the Republic of Serb Krajina and other bodies of the executive, and then there was also a system of courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As you mentioned the government of the SAO Krajina and then the Republic of Serbian Krajina, or the executive branch, what were the main ministries? Can you enumerate at least some of them?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government of the SAO Krajina, and later on the Republic of Serbian Krajina, had all the standard ministries that exist in all countries; the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of the Interior, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Information, the Ministry of Trade, all the usual ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: From 1991 to 1995, you were a deputy in the assembly. Do you know whether the government of the SAO Krajina and then of the Republic of Serbian Krajina had any sessions, whether it operated, and whether the Prime Minister carried out his job?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the period from the 19th of December, 1990, when the SAO Krajina was established, until the 4th of August, 1995, the government worked normally. It had its sessions, it adopted decisions, it tabled bills in the assembly, just like any other government anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As you held an important political office in the Serb Democratic Party on the one hand and as you were a deputy in the assembly, first of the SAO Krajina and then of the Republic of Serbian Krajina on the other hand, can you tell us whether, apart from the regular government organs, the official ones, there was a kind of parallel secret or clandestine organisation or programme aimed at perpetrating crimes and mistreating the Croatian population, persecuting, incarcerating and killing the Serbian -- the non-Serbian population? Did this exist on the territory of the Krajina as a kind of parallel system?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert decisively that there was no plan, no secret criminal organisation or anything of the kind you've described. My answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When yesterday we followed the chronology of events, we arrived at the end of 1991. We mentioned the conflicts on the territory of the then Yugoslav Republic of Croatia. Do you know in what period of time UNPROFOR was deployed and the so-called Vance Plan was implemented?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The negotiations concerning the Vance Plan, in order to limit them in time, took place in late 1991, in November and December, 1991, and in early 1992. As far as I can recall, the final result was the adoption of the Vance Plan and Resolution 743 of the Security Council, whereby peacekeeping forces of the United Nations were deployed. They were referred to as UNPROFOR. As far as I can recall, their deployment began in March, 1992, and this went on for several months until the deployment was complete, in four sectors; north, south, east and west, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, Mr. Licina, whether the organs of the SAO Krajina, the cabinet, the assembly - and I wish to explain right away that I am referring to the organs that existed on the ground - some people call it the so-called SAO Krajina, but in any case, there were organs operating on the ground, and I want to know whether the organs of the SAO Krajina and the Republic of Serb Krajina, at the time the peacekeeping forces arrived, respected, complied with, and implemented the UN resolution and the Vance Plan. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, all the elements of the Vance Plan were respected by the Republic of Serb Krajina. When some people say the so-called organs, I wish to say that the previous state of Croatia was practically divided into two. The two nations had created two states, in fact, one of them, however, was not internationally recognised but the Republic of Serb Krajina was in fact a state. It had its executive, legislative, and judiciary government; it had its territory which it controlled; it had all the characteristics of a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In view of your reply, the then Republic of Croatia was recognised in January, 1992. Can one call that the so-called Republic of Croatia in relation to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One could apply the same criterion and refer to it as so-called. The difference was that the Krajina controlled the territory it considered its own, whereas Croatia was not in control of the territory it considered its own at the time, so it was questionable whether it was a state in the full meaning of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Serb Krajina put its weapons under a double key in UNPROFOR-controlled warehouses?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of this, yes. This is correct. So-called blue battalions were established under Resolution 743. Only police forces could exist under that resolution, so the so-called blue battalions were established. Most of us then left the army. We were no longer in the military, no longer carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When the UN troops arrived, the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Serb Krajina, or its army, did it have heavy weapons, heavy artillery, mortars and so on, and were these heavy weapons put in warehouses?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Heavy weapons were put in warehouses, although very soon Resolution 743 and the Vance Plan were violated. All the UNPROFOR forces hadn't even been deployed yet when the Vance Plan was violated and there was an attack in Dalmatia; more precisely, on the Miljevac plateau. This happened in June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Miljevac plateau which you mentioned, was it supposed to be under United Nations protection?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Miljevac plateau was an area which, according to the plan, was supposed to be protected by UN forces. Croatia, however, carried out an aggression on this area. As far as I know, about 150 people were killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this operation by the Croatian army on the Miljevac plateau, do you know whether the Security Council passed any resolutions in this connection?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the resolution or that there was a resolution. I know that some warnings were issued, but Croatia was encouraged by this to continue violating the Vance Plan and Resolution 743, so there was only an oral reprimand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Croatian forces withdraw from the Miljevac plateau where they had arrived in violation of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they didn't. There was more than one such incursion before the final attack and occupation of the Republic of Serb Krajina in Operation Storm. I know that the police and military forces never returned to any area where there was an incursion, and there were other such incursions in September, 1992, in Miljevac Polje [phoen], then in Maslenica in January, 1993, in the Medak pocket in September, 1993, and later on, there was Operation Flash in Western Slavonia in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the UN peacekeeping forces, the blue helmets, have an obligation to protect the entire population in the UN protected areas and free them of fear of an armed attack? Did they have such an obligation or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection. Leading question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Leading question, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I asked the witness whether there was or was not such an obligation. We can reformulate the question but ... I will do that if Your Honour so decides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You dispute that you made an objectionable statement. If you want to rephrase, are you admitting that you made an objectionable statement? If you do, then you've got to withdraw the previous one and then rephrase. I'm not sure whether you are saying you're admitting or not admitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order to gain time, I withdraw this question and I will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't wish to be seen as putting leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, the resolution of the Security Council under which the UN forces arrived on the territory of Yugoslavia contains several elements. Did any of these elements contain an obligation relating to protection of these areas?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, and in view of the way in which the arrival of the UN peacekeeping forces was received, it was explained to us - and that was our understanding of the resolution - that the peacekeeping forces were supposed to give full protection to the population in the areas where they were deployed. That was the area of the Republic of Serb Krajina, divided into those four sectors, as they were called then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And in your opinion, did the UN fulfil its obligation, for example, in the Miljevac plateau?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's evident that the UN peacekeeping forces did not fulfil this obligation, and not just in the Miljevac plateau but in any of the later Croatian offensives. Terrible crimes were committed, large numbers of people were killed in all these Croatian aggressions. The peacekeeping forces would turn up after a Croatian aggression as a kind of buffer zone, when we had practically already been expelled from those areas. For this reason, I feel that the peacekeeping forces failed to comply with their obligation contained in the resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: There is an important question in these proceedings and that is the question of long-barrelled weapons, automatic rifles, which the police of the Republika Srpska Krajina or the SAO Krajina carried. Can you please tell us why the SAO Krajina police had automatic rifles in spite of the fact that there were troops in the protected zone of the UN? There were 11.000 of such troops.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I said, the peace forces began to deploy in March, 1992, and this deployment took several months to be completed. The deployment was not completed, of the peacekeeping forces, when they were already some violations of the plan and the violations of the resolution by an attack on the Miljevac plateau in June, so not a full three months later. The peacekeeping forces had still not deployed, we had placed our weaponry under lock and key, so in that situation it would have been absolute folly to disarm completely. It was quite logical to keep the long-barrelled weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, in spite of this aggression on the Miljevac plateau, you mentioned several other major activities by the Croatian armed forces in the UN protected zones. Other than those large actions, which had their names, these aggressions, were there any other conflicts? And if so, when, and how many? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are four major Croatian offensives that are known: The Miljevac plateau, Miljevac Polje was a slightly smaller action. After that, in January, there was Maslenica -- in January, 1993. In September, 1993, there was the Medak pocket in the Lika area; and in May, 1995, there was Operation Flash in Western Slavonia. Other than that, there were constant separate attacks, but we remember this as four major offensives. Constantly, from the fighting at the Miljevac plateau until the occupation of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in August, 1995, there was constant fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you talk about this question, this constant fighting, can you tell us whether this is something that you experienced personally or was this something that you received as a member of parliament or in some other way? What is your source of information? You say that you were in Gracac. The Republic of the territory of the SAO Krajina is much larger than the place where you were.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a member of parliament of SAO Krajina, of course it's natural that I was informed about these things. As far as my personal experiences, there were such cases in my municipality every day. The municipality of Gracac is small in territory but it has 13.000 -- its population is about 13.000. In the war it lost about 500 of its inhabitants, so I did have plenty of occasions to attend funerals. I knew most of these people. So I did have a lot of information about these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have information about how it was possible that the Croatian soldiers, police, simply crossed the line of separation, entered the UN protected areas, in circumstances when there were about 10 to 11.000 soldiers out in the field? How was something like that possible? What were these other soldiers doing? What was happening to them? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, they stood at the sidelines. When you ask me this, it's not clear to me how this is possible. This is something that should not have been possible, but evidently it did happen. It's one thing what was actually signed, what was on paper, and what the top organ, the Security Council of the United Nations, declared, and it was quite another thing what was happening in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As for what was happening in the field, there are many UN documents as well as documents by the UNPROFOR civilian police about the suffering of the Croatian population in the area of the SAO Krajina, for which the police forces of SAO Krajina are charged. Can you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have information about that from the newspapers. I know that I think Franjo Tudjman - and I have that here in the text - that Franjo Tudjman said that Croatia lost 13.000 -- no, 10.000 people, that there were 10.000 victims from Croatia. But no Serbian casualties were given there. So when he spoke about casualties and victims, he was talking exclusively about Croatians. If you look at the number of the population, proportionally, of Croatia and Krajina, the ratio of the victims is three times greater on the Krajina side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When I mentioned the UNPROFOR report, is it true that the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina and its police had a plan and tortured, killed, and detained the Croatian population deliberately?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such case. I have not heard about anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned several attacks on the UN Protected Area. Can you tell us whether in that period, from late 1991 and early 1992, when the resolution on the mission of the United Nations in Yugoslavia was adopted and until Operation Storm, was there any assault operation carried out by the army or police of the Republika Srpska Krajina against the Croatian side whereby it would have to cross the line of separation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the army of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, the police - so the police and the army as regular forces of the Republic of Serbian Krajina - in that period did not carry out any assault operations. No advance was made in that sense. The only thing that happened was the aggression on the territory of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the Miljevac plateau in January, 1993. You mentioned also the Maslenica operation and the Medak pocket. Can you tell us what the position was of the civilian population in that area, in the areas that were attacked by the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the operation on the Maslenica bridge in Ravni Kotari, there was a major pogrom of the civilian population in Ravni Kotari, in the villages of Smokovic, Kasic, and others. In this operation, I think that there were about 300 casualties. At the same time, when this operation in the Maslenica area was being carried out, there was also a terrorist incursion in the Gracac municipality area, in the sector of Mali Alan [phoen]. I think that that location is called Egeljac. Croatian forces entered that area, they intercepted a truck full of soldiers of the RSK, and they carried out a bestial crime in which 22 soldiers were slaughtered. Their throats were cut. It was an evident killing. Later, during the post-mortem, it was established that the cause of death was a cold weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened to the property, the houses, the churches, in the-- belonging to the Serbian population in the villages that were attacked by the Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb property was looted, robbed, burned, and buildings were also treated in the same way as well as church property, Orthodox church buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the Security Council reacted in any way to this operation in the Maslenica area and if the Croat side suffered any consequences because of that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no consequences for the Croatian side regarding this matter. It all once again boiled down to a very mild warning, and Croatia, with such an approach by the United Nations, was practically encouraged to continue with more crimes against the people of the Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the Medak pocket area is, which villages make up that area and what happened in September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the Medak pocket. It is located practically in the territory of the Gracac municipality. These were Serb villages that had joined the Gracac municipality. This is something that I spoke about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was this a protected area, area under the protection of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was under the protection of the UN peacekeeping forces. These are villages Divoselo, Pocitelj, Ornice, and Citluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened in that area? Do you have information about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since at the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection. I'm sorry for the interruption, Your Honour. I didn't object to this previously because I thought it may be a short topic, but I wonder what the relevance of all this is, especially if -- you know, if the witness wants to mention that there were these incursions, I don't object to that, but the details of what happened to the civilian population, and the details of attacks, Croats versus Serbs, I don't see how that relates to the charges in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The testimony of this witness is something that the Defence is using to point to the nature of reports of the United Nations that were sent to the Security Council, in which there is very little or there are practically no details about what was happening in the UN protected zone in situations when there was enormous suffering by the civilian population. One-sided reports were being sent, in the opinion of the Defence. Of course, we cannot comment on that but we would like to present the actual situation in the field. And we think that this is a very relevant question because it also connects to the main point of the Prosecution about the joint criminal enterprise. And this testimony could be an answer to many matters initiated by the Prosecution in their case. It has to do with the weaponry amongst the Krajina Police, the presence of the military in Krajina, the conduct of the UN forces, so the conduct of all the parties. So the Defence disputes the position of the Prosecution on these matters and believes that UN reports were not objective and that they were partial. In order to substantiate these claims, it's necessary to put to the witness question about the key events which were even registered in some UN Security Council resolutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If I could respond, Your Honour. If the point were to impugn the United Nations reports, why haven't we seen any United Nations reports? These reports exist. We have some, many have been disclosed to the Defence. But they don't use them. The Defence prefers to put on its case by having witness talk about things, about speeches, about reports. We never get to actually see those reports. I suggest that what is really going on here is that, as usual, the Defence is trying to focus on the actions of the Croatian forces instead of focusing on the crimes charged in the indictment. If they are really attacking the UN reports, I think we should see those reports. As to the relevance of this material to the JCE, I think that's minimal at best. The Prosecution's case is that the JCE was formed certainly by 1990, 1991. All of these matters are later than that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black, I thought -- I don't know. My -- let me put it this way: The Defence has really never declared what their defence is in this case. We've just been trying to read it in between the lines. But what you allege is what they are trying to do, namely to show what the Croats did the Serbs, is consistent with what they have been doing from the beginning, and this Tribunal, or rather, this Chamber has tried to find out exactly what the defence is, and without being told by the Defence, it becomes very difficult to know whether any question is relevant or not relevant. But to the extent that the Chamber has been able to read in between the lines, that seems to be the defence of the Defence: You did it, we did it too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position is that that -- it may be their defence, but it's not a legally valid defence. The fact that they did it too cannot possibly affect Mr. Martic's criminal responsibility for the crimes alleged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But then, if I rule in your favour, then they must close their case. There is nothing else to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: They would either have to close their case or find a legally justifiable Defence because there is no sense in having 260 more hours of a Defence case on a defence that is not a defence, it has no legal bearing on the case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this argument not a little too late in the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I've tried to object as we went along, Your Honour. I think Mr. Whiting and other members of counsel have objected to these very types of questions. Whenever the questioning on cross-examination went to crimes against Serbs by Croats, or went beyond the allegations in the indictment, we've tried to object without being overly -- trying not to disrupt the flow of trial, Your Honour, but we have objected to this constantly throughout the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Black, there might be a further point, though, because, as Mr. Milovancevic has said, when the Prosecution's case was continuing, there was evidence coming from Prosecution witnesses concerning the Vance Plan and surrounding circumstances, and the UNPROFOR forces, and it gave a particular perspective that could have been said to reflect that the Serbs were the aggressors and the Croats were the persons who were on the receiving end, and it did lend a different perspective that was consistent with the Prosecution's case. I believe that what Mr. Milovancevic is saying, while that factually was incorrect, it is irrelevant in determination of the issues and what we the Defence are attempting to do now is to give you, from our position, the correct view to show that the Serbs were not in fact the aggressors and that it was the Croatians in those circumstances. So there was -- there would be a point of relevance. I think it extends beyond the mere you did it to us, we did it to you. So from that perspective, I would say that there is relevance, and at the end of the day, it would be part of what would be before the Court in resolving certain issues that are necessary to determine the guilt or innocence on to those relevant counts in the indictment. So that would be my own perspective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just wanted to add that, from the point of view of the Defence - and again this is what one would try to read in between the lines - that it's some kind of self-defence. That's -- so whether it is, we will find out at the end, but this is how I read it as it goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I would agree also. Thank you, Judge Moloto.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I have just a few seconds to confer with counsel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could I briefly respond, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The first point is hopefully to clarify. The Prosecution case has never been that the Croatian side does not violate the Vance Plan or that there was not a military conflict, including in the pink zones, which are the areas that are being discussed here. We have tried to focus on the treatment of Croatian civilians within the territory of the RSK. That's been the focus of our case. And I think most importantly, self-defence is not a defence to war crimes and crimes against humanity against those Croat civilians in the RSK. That I think is clear from the jurisprudence which I believe we've cited in a filing, and of course the parties will cite in their final briefs, but whether or not this whole discussion -- I accept that it has some -- it does have some relevance to the Vance Plan, and if that's the -- if that's the reason for putting this forward, certainly I accept that it has some relevance, although I would question the devotion of so much time to this which is really -- it's a very, very marginal matter, has limited or no significance to the Prosecution case, and we did not -- it was never part of the Prosecution case that the Croatian side did not violate the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I would agree with you, Mr. Black, save and except that quite a bit of evidence has come before the Court on the Prosecution side, factually, and as that is the case, I think it would not be in the interest of justice in my own view - I do not know if my brothers would agree with me - to then limit the Defence when the Prosecution has, if even incidentally to the several legal issues, it has led quite a bit of evidence for the Defence to contradict. So as that was part and parcel of the Prosecution case, I do believe that, in fairness, in the interest of justice and a fair trial, that correspondingly, howsoever, the Defence itself must now be given the opportunity to air these issues and to respond and to put before the Trial Chamber what it considers is its own case and its own responses to the facts. So from that perspective, whilst acknowledging your position as to how your case was structured and how it was placed before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Once again -- excuse me. I just want to add a little point here. No matter how insignificant a point may have been from the point of view of the Prosecution, it is up to the Defence to interpret it, and if from their perspective it's an important point, they must be given an opportunity to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I won't take any more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The objection is overruled. Mr. Milovancevic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, you said that the Medak pocket area was under the UN protection. What happened to the population during the operation called Medak pocket? What happened to the Serb civilian population?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said previously, the Medak pocket covers the four villages that I enumerated, with other hamlets. In September of 1993, there was an incursion of Croatian forces. As I remember, even based on the reports of General Jean Cot, who was a member of the UN peacekeeping forces, in that area, after the Croatian operation, nothing living was left. Everything was destroyed. The soldiers, civilians, and animals were killed, and that whole area of Medak pocket was basically an area of scorched earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, do you know whether there were any negotiations between the RSK representatives with the Croatian side, any negotiations that were facilitated either by UNPROFOR or international negotiators?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, usually during the negotiations held between the Serbian and Croatian side, it was precisely then that such incursions occurred. If I remember well, the then Prime Minister, Djordje Bjegovic, was taking part in negotiations in London or some place else precisely during the time when the Medak pocket operation was carried out. And I need to add that there were some 100 people killed in the Medak pocket area. These people are mostly from my municipality, Gracac municipality, and Donji Lapac municipality, so that means that I knew personally quite a number of victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the so-called Zagreb agreement? Do you know what provisions it had? The agreement I think was concluded on the 29th of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Zagreb agreement was signed in 1994. It regulated the early stages of economic cooperation between the Serbs and Croats. I think that it regulated the use of highway and gas pipeline, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I had in mind a kind of a military agreement which stipulated the separation of forces. You were referring to an economic agreement. Do you distinguish between the two?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you can't do that. I'm sorry. The witness has given you an answer. It's an economic cooperation. What does military agreement come into it? Are you not -- do you want to take the stand? He's answered you. What you had in mind, you keep in your mind. Carry on with the economic cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now that you've mentioned the economic cooperation, Mr. Licina, were any provisions on economic cooperation implemented?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the highway was opened for traffic in Western Slavonia. And the Zagreb agreement had a number of levels. One of them was the economic one, and then there was the military aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to deny you talking on the military agreement part of it. Okay? Deal with the economic agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, where were you in May of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May of 1995, I was in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned the Operation Flash, can you tell us, what was your source of information concerning that operation, and can you describe to us briefly what happened and in which area?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've told you, I was a member of parliament and a member of the security board. In May of 1995, there was an incursion of Croatian forces, which was another aggression of Croatia carried out against the RSK and yet another violation of the Vance Plan. They made an incursion into the territory of Western Slavonia. I believe it was Sector West. They completely cleansed out ethnically the municipalities of Pakrac and Okucani, and there was a pogrom in Western Slavonia in 1991 as well, at which time the Serbs were cleansed out of the area of Grubisno Polje, Podravska Slatina, and Daruvar, which is to say that the whole area was cleansed out of Serbs, which carried with it quite a lot of victims. Later on, we learned that many victims were burned in caves in Sisak and other places. However, this is all second-hand information, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When the police and other forces attacked Western Slavonia, was that area under the UN protection?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, that area was under the control of the UN. This came after the political turmoil which surrounded the so-called Z-4 plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Croatian army and police ever withdraw from Western Slavonia? They attacked the UN protected area, they killed civilians. Did the Security Council react to such a grave violation of international law?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. Once again I think there was a verbal reprimand; however, Croatian forces remained there and were basically given green light to carry out the later aggression against the RSK in August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar of any -- familiar with any aspects of the Z-4 plan? When was it drafted and what was its fate?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This plan originated in late 1994 and early 1995. The Z-4 plan was offered earlier, back when -- in 1992, Croatia, under pressure from international community, came up with a proposal to redefine Croatia. I think that they had a constitutional law on establishing counties of Glina and some other counties, and then this plan was just renamed into the Z-4 plan and was offered to the Republic of Serbian Krajina later. This, however, was happening at the same time when the mandate of UNPROFOR was extended. President Martic at that time informed us, saying that the plan would be discussed when the status of UN forces was going to be discussed, and that was completely logical at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Before you proceed, who is President Martic? Mr. Licina, could you please answer this question? I don't know if the evidence has been led before and I missed it. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milan Martic was elected president in 1994, in January, if I'm not mistaken, and he's present here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the question put by Her Honour Nosworthy, you said that Martic was elected president. President of what?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was elected president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether there were any Serb victims in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, there were a large number of victims in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It's Western Slavonia, not Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a report of the Veritas centre detailing that there were about 1.000 victims, or missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the exact number of victims was ever established?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exact number of victims was never established. We, as the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in exile, have some figures which we received from the documentation and information centre Veritas. These are victims and these are the people who were reported as missing by their family members, so this is quite beyond dispute, and Veritas uses the number of 6.500 of those who were killed or went missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You are referring to the number of 6.500 of those who were killed and gone missing. During which period of time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1991 to 1995, in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. These are the citizens of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. As this was taking place, we recorded the names of these people as those who were victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is centre Veritas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documentation and information centre Veritas is a non-governmental organisation collecting information about the victims in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. It is headed by Mr. Savo Strbac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And does your information that you have just been giving us emanate from that source, from that organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What I just said, yes. However, based on our information, the number of victims is even greater. However, in view of the circumstances under which we conduct our work, it was impossible for us to collect the precise information because our people are living everywhere throughout the world. The family members would come to the Veritas centre and report their relatives as missing or killed. This is the basis on which this information was compiled. Since the centre was established back in 1992 or 1993, that means that it was operative during that period of time and information was collected at the time, and then later, also it was done regarding the events in 1995 in May and in August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, how -- in what form did you receive this information from Veritas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the form of charts. I have one such chart here with me. They have regular bulletins that they publish. As far as I'm aware, the documentation and information centre Veritas has good cooperation with this Tribunal and it sends its reports regularly to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the Operation Storm, Mr. Licina. What does this term denote?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Operation Storm denotes an aggression of Croatian army on the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. To be more precise, the territory of the old SAO Krajina, which is Northern Dalmatia, Kordun, Lika, and Krajina. This operation started in August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what was the outcome of that operation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The outcome of that operation is definitely the greatest case of ethnic cleansing in Europe after the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt the witness. At this point I have to object. This is August of 1995. Your Honours, I believe, have already ruled that whatever happened to Serbs, whatever was done to Serbs by Croatians in Operation Storm is not relevant to this indictment. It can't even be self-defence because it happens after all of the alleged crimes in this indictment. There is no basis for this, Your Honour, in our submission; it's simply not relevant to the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the indictment covers the period from 1991 until the end of 1995. Mr. Martic is charged in this indictment for participation in joint criminal enterprise throughout that period of time. Earlier, when objecting earlier, my learned friend explained that this was the joint criminal enterprise carried out in the period 1991 to 1992. If they wish to amend the indictment, then I would be very glad to hear that. However, the indictment states that the joint criminal enterprise period was in place throughout the end of 1995. During that period of time, there were some events which happened which are mentioned in their indictment. In the final paragraphs of the indictment, 69 and 70 - I may be wrong about the number of the paragraph - they mention the Operation Storm and they say that by means of that operation, the Croatian government established its authority in the territory of Krajina. This act, which was an attack under the UN protected zone, the Prosecutor described this as an event where the civilian population withdrew with the military and we wonder how come they withdrew with the military? This is something that we disagree with in the indictment. This is one of the key issues that we disagree about, and by omitting precisely such issues, they come to some other conclusions with which we disagree as well. Once again, for the umpteenth time, the Defence has to prove that it would be incredible and naive for us to defend a crime with another crime. This is not the strategy of our defence, no. The Defence is trying to show that there existed throughout the time a joint criminal enterprise on the Croatian side and that the Serbian population from the beginning to the end only tried to protect itself and that, despite the United Nations, the outcome was a Serbian exodus. The events are portrayed in a different manner here. Whether there were any individual crimes throughout that period of time, that's another issue. Maybe the Prosecutor can give us example of a war where there were no individual crimes. Now we are discussing a topic which arose on the basis of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just ask, Mr. Milovancevic, that when you deal with an objection, please try to focus on the objection and don't deal with the entire case. But I've heard what you said. Yes, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could respond briefly. The first point is Defence counsel has made reference, I believe, to paragraph 78 of the indictment. There is a reference to Operation Storm. As I read it now, at no point does the Prosecution describe this as an event where the civilian population withdrew with the military. That's not something that we represented in the indictment, which is what Defence counsel says at line 18 of page 26. Operation Storm is mentioned in the additional fact section of the indictment because obviously that was when the RSK ended, but the last -- and it's quite right, Defence counsel is right that the indictment period extends up to December, 1995. That is mostly done to reflect the possibility of 7(3) liability extending, the failure to punish, even after criminal incidents, but the last criminal incident alleged in the indictment is the 3rd of May, 1995, the shelling of Zagreb. I cannot understand how Operation Storm could justify any of those incidents, the shelling of Zagreb or any incident before, nor do I understand how a Croatian operation in August, 1995, has a bearing on the JCE, even if it did extend to the end of 1995, as alleged in the indictment. The Prosecution has no intention of amending its indictment to shorten the period of the JCE. What I said, or meant to say before, is that it's been clear from the Prosecution case that the JCE was in place by 1990 or 1991, therefore it could not have been a response to events that happened in 1993 and 1994 and 1995. If the Defence case is to allege a Croat JCE, I would suggest that's another case, not this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber will rule on the objection when we come back from the break. Can we come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: If I may ask you, Mr. Milovancevic, how much further -- yes. Mr. Milovancevic, how much further do you intend to address these issues related to Operation Storm for the establishing -- for establishing your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, very briefly and very concisely. Very briefly, very concisely, and the Defence has more than one task in this respect. One of these is to check what the OTP expert Mr. Grujic has said about the number of victims. These statements are drastically different from the facts that the Defence has at its disposal, and we wish to point to the actual state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your question, Mr. Milovancevic, was what was the outcome of the Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, when you talk about the number of victims, are you talking about number of victims during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. The number of victims in the findings of the expert is part of the information presented to the Chamber, and I want to see with this witness whether it's part of the information presented by the witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question is then allowed. The objection will be overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, can you briefly tell us what the outcome of Operation Storm was with respect to the civilian population on the territory covered by that operation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said previously, Operation Storm completely ethnically cleansed the areas of Northern Dalmatia, Kordun, Lika, and Banija of the Serb population. There were some 250.000 refugees. As for victims, according to the information I have, there were over a thousand. I don't have the precise number in my memory. A hundred -- no, 1.909, according to the Veritas information. This is confirmed by my own experience. I said previously that Gracac municipality, in this war, suffered 500 casualties. About 200 of these were in Gracac municipality alone. Gracac municipality is one of 15 municipalities affected by this operation. This illustrates the extent of the crime that was perpetrated here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just state a concern, Mr. Milovancevic. I see Mr. Licina has a blue-looking plastic in front of him which seems to be a document cover. And he keeps looking at it. I'm not quite sure what is happening. I would have thought that he's testifying from memory. I'm not quite sure what the status of the document he keeps on looking at is. Are you able to clarify this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, you heard His Honour's question, the question by the Presiding Judge. You said that you had some information at your disposal. Can you tell us what is in your blue file?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said previously when talking about the Veritas documentation and information centre, which deals with victims on the territory of the Republic of Serb Krajina, this is an excerpt from the Veritas bulletin. It's true that I am testifying according to memory, but I cannot keep all the numbers in my head, which is why I brought this along, in order to refresh my memory as far as numbers are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are not allowed to use a document which has no status before this Court to refresh your memory and you're not testifying as an expert witness, are you? He's not testifying as an expert witness, Mr. Milovancevic; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. I will ask the witness not to use this document. He has just taken it out. He took it out when he started discussing the numbers of victims. This is the witness's own documentation, which we are neither using nor tendering at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's precisely why it should not be used. Can you put it in your bag, please, Mr. Licina. Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, where were you on the 4th of August, 1995, the day Operation Storm started?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 4th of August, 1995, I was in Gracac. That morning, the shelling began. As far as I can recall, at about 5.00 in the morning. That was when the attack began. As I learned later, this was an all-out Croatian attack on the Krajina, the first axis of attack taken by the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, please, as we are now not going into the details of the operation, I wish to ask you not to continue with this in order not to take up time, but all I want to know is your experience. Can you tell us whether Gracac was both a town and a municipality in the UN protected areas and whether there were any military facilities. Because you say there was artillery fire on the town in the morning.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gracac was one of 27 municipalities in the Republic of Serb Krajina. It's in the area of Lika. The town of Gracac is the seat of Gracac municipality. In the town itself, there were no military forces or any military facilities. Our closest forces were some 15 or 20 kilometres away from the town in the areas of Mali Alan, Metka, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And who opened artillery fire? You say shelling began. Who opened fire on that town and other towns?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Croatian army, the Croatian forces. The shelling of Gracac -- well, Gracac had been shelled before this, but that day was the most intensive shelling. Gracac had been shelled continuously for months before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'll just put one more question to you about this. What happened to you and the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like most people from the Krajina, in those few days I was part of the column leaving for Serbia. We left because of the pressure of the Croatian aggression. To the best of my knowledge, about 250.000 people left. And a huge area was completely ethnically cleansed. This was the end of a series of events which had lasted for a little under five years, during which over 600.000 Serbs left Croatia. An entire nation was ethnically cleansed from a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, with respect to the Vance Plan which we mentioned, the resolution by which this plan was adopted and UN troops deployed on the territory of Yugoslavia was Resolution 743, as you said. Do you know whether the Croatian side accepted the Vance Plan, and was the Croatian side obliged to comply with it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was. Because the Croatian side also agreed to it. It was only after the agreement of both sides that the resolution began to be implemented. It was, however, broken by the Croatian side very soon, only a few months after the deployment of the UN troops. I have already mentioned the events on the Miljevac plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that all this ended with Operation Storm, my next question is you mentioned the number of 650 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 6.500.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: -- people who were killed in this period between 1991 and 1995. Does this number of 6.500 people killed also include those killed during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in part. As I said, the documentation and information centre Veritas collected this information by interviewing members of families of people who were killed or missing, who came to the Veritas centre to report this. There was also a large movement of our people who went to third countries. So I believe this information to be incomplete. I think the numbers are higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because there was an official of the Republic of Croatia who testified here, Mr. Grujic, who in his expert testimony said that there were 302 Serb victims in the territory of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does this refer only to the Storm Operation or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: As I recall Mr. Grujic's testimony, and I hope counsel will correct me if I'm wrong and point me to the transcript, he did not say there were only 302 Serb victims to Operation Storm. What he said was -- I think he referred to that number as some that he was aware of, but he made no representations as to the entire amount of victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecution provided the parties and the Chamber with an expert finding where it is explicitly said that there are 302 Serbian victims and about 4.150 persons whose identity and ethnicity were not established. The Defence has tried to test this question by putting questions to the expert, but we didn't get an answer other than getting an additional explanation that some people were later exhumed and identified, but the identification process was not completed, so it is not known who these persons are. This is why I am discussing these figures which seem to be drastically different from the testimony of this witness. I'm just trying, at least, to make a very brief comparison. This is why I put this question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My problem is that this witness has already said that he believes the information that he has to be incomplete, that he thinks the numbers are higher. And your question related to the number 6.500 dead, dead people, which, according to your question, as I understood it, are not entirely from Operation Storm. You asked the question, "Does that number include the number killed in Desert Storm [sic]." Maybe you can ask the witness how many, according to him, were killed in Desert Storm, if he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will put the question in such a way. I think that perhaps you didn't quite understand what I was asking. So to avoid providing an explanation, I'm going to put the question in such a way that the witness can answer. With your permission, Your Honour, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Continue and let's hear what you're going to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, can you tell us, what is the information that you have at your disposal about the number of casualties amongst the population of the Serb ethnicity in Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that I have is 1.900 casualties. This number that I mentioned, 6.500, refers to the overall casualties throughout the war, produced by the Veritas centre. Earlier I said that only in the territory of my municipality about 200 people were killed during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, when you refer to 6.500 victims, are you talking about Serbian victims in RSK territory? Is this clear?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I talk about casualties, 6.500 casualties that the Veritas centre reported, I'm talking about casualties who were citizens of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. We did not split these by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you now a refugee by status, Mr. Licina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Other than you, are there any other persons of Serb ethnicity who fled during Flash and Storm who still have that status?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I said before, over 600.000 people fled the territory of Croatia, primarily Serbs, people of Serb ethnicity, who found refuge mostly in Serbia, Republika Srpska, and other countries. In the meantime, the state of Serbia defined the status people had to have identity papers issued in order to get a job and for other purposes. So at the moment, only 7.000 people have status refugee, of refugees, although the other people who were issued with identity papers are still practically refugees because they did not manage to secure their other rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You're saying that when they received their new identity papers in another country, they lost their status of refugees, although they still remain in that status?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. They lost their status, so the official figure of the number of refugees in Serbia today is 107.000, but I think there are at least three times as many people who are actually refugees but they had to take out new identity papers because of jobs, because of property issues, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, I have some other questions before we finish. At the beginning of your testimony you explained the attempt by political representatives of the Serbian people in Croatia to resolve the status of the Serbian people in Croatia in a legal way, something that would also be covered by constitutional articles, but it has been said that the Serbian population was frightened by genocide, that their fears were incited through the media, through speeches of politicians, various newspaper articles, and writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I don't see a question here. I see a speech. It seems like Defence counsel is testifying. Perhaps I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have that problem, Mr. Milovancevic, and you're beginning to talk about genocide and other fears. I'm not quite sure whether you're asking a question or what you're doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will put a very short question to the witness so that I would not make such an impression, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That would be very helpful. And while we are at the question of short questions, may I just also ask the witness to give short, concise answers to the question. I've been trying to hold myself from saying so, to allow you to say what you have to say as a witness, but most of your questions [sic] are also very lengthy and go far beyond what is asked. The details, if your counsel wants them, he will get them by asking follow-up questions. Try to concentrate on the question and answer the question. Do the same, Mr. Milovancevic. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, you were a high official of the SDS. You were a member of parliament throughout the time you were in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina since the beginning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I must interrupt you once again, Mr. Milovancevic. All that is already on record. We know he was a high official and just put the question so that your question is short. Don't prefix it with a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, at the party and state level, at the RSK, in the activity of the organs, was there any false fear created by them amongst the population of the danger of genocide or the allegedly dangerous Ustasha or non-Ustasha state?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No organ ever, either of the SDS party or of all the other state organs of the RSK and the SAO Krajina, ever generated fear. What it was actually about were actually facts that were evident to all. Croatia, without the Serbs, embarked on a redefinition of its state. It redefined its constitution without the agreement of the Serbs, and the Serbs were absolutely forced to make their own political moves. All the moves made by the Serbian leadership in Krajina were forced as a result of the activity by Croatia, such as the forming of the SAO Krajina, which was done when the Croatian constitution was adopted. The referendum in Krajina was held at the time that Croatia had its referendum on secession from Yugoslavia. Croatia violated all international laws with these major offensives and attacks on territory that were under the protection of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Licina, your answer to the question is contained in the first sentence. Then you made another 11 to 12 sentences, which really don't answer the question. So what I'm trying to suggest to you, listen to the question, answer the question. If any more detail is required of you, the counsel will ask you questions. We are trying to finish this case as soon as we possibly can and if we are going to be listening to long speeches that are not answers to questions, we are not likely to finish. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have completed my examination-in-chief. I have allowed the witness to finish these few sentences, considering that to be an explanation of what he said in the first sentence. Thank you very much, Your Honours. And I thank the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I start, Your Honour, I would like to register a complaint, in a sense. A great deal of what this witness has testified about is not contained in the Rule 65 summary. What we would request is in the future, if there is also going to be additional information which is not contained in the Rule 65 ter summary, that we could have supplemental information sheets. Your Honours may be aware or may recall that that's what the Prosecution does during its case. Of course, it's slightly different circumstances. The Defence has a statement, et cetera. But when we interview the witness again and meet with them for proofing, if any new material comes out and we realise new material is going to be addressed in court, we provide that ahead of time to the Defence, and we would ask that a similar practice be adopted by the Defence to help us prepare, essentially, for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You heard that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is also in our interests to behave in the same way, and we are absolutely in favour of having the proceedings conducted in the proper way, absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it correct that you asked questions that you didn't -- on topics you hadn't mentioned in the 65 ter summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We kept to the topics that we mentioned in our summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's a point of -- that's a disputed point now. We'll have to have a look at the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Would you like me to go through it, Your Honours? I hope my memory serves me. For instance, I do recall at least one mention of Mr. Martic as being the president, his position on the Vance Plan. I think Her Honour Judge Nosworthy asked a question about that. Mr. Martic is mentioned nowhere in the 65 ter summary. There were questions about the different organs of the RSK government, the different ministries, judicial branch, et cetera. Nowhere does that appear in the 65 ter summary. The Vance Plan is mentioned only in passing when it says in June, 1992, several months following the adoption of the Vance Plan, there was a massacre in Miljevac plateau. That's the only reference to the Vance Plan and yet there was quite a bit of discussion of the Vance Plan. Also, you remember the Defence counsel said one of their main points was to show that UN documents were not accurate. I don't see any reference to any UN documents. Another problem, Your Honour, it may be part of the confusion or misunderstanding between counsel, is that although these are the revised 65 ter summaries, there is a lot of statement of topics. For instance, it says the witness sets out facts on the arms supplied to the Croats. What we heard about was Spegelj, and we heard about different things about arming, but that's not mentioned in the 65 ter summary. What we have is a reference to the topic of arms supplied to Croats. Those are just a few examples, Your Honour. If you want a comprehensive review, I think I would have to take more time maybe at the break to list them all out, but I think the point is made there were a number of topics that weren't addressed in the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any response to that, Mr. Milovancevic? Maybe my brother and sister might have copies, but I personally don't have a copy of the 65 ter statement at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have one copy, if that would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've received a copy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I guess it's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't see any reference to Operation Storm in this summary, Mr. Milovancevic. On the contrary, I see a reference to Operation Flash.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence believes that it did not exceed in any question the gist of the information it provided to the Prosecution. It did mention a whole series of topics to be dealt with with this witness. The answers of the witness are impossible to predict fully so that the answer would then be able to be incorporated into the information that we provided to the Prosecution. The Defence believes that as far as the information it provided to the Prosecution, it did stick to the main essential topics that were mentioned in the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber has just made you aware that there is no reference to Operation Storm in your summary and there was an extensive cross-examination -- leading by you on Operation Storm. I don't intend to take this matter any further. That point alone justifies the Bench in reiterating the request of the Prosecution, by way of a warning to you, that if you intend going beyond what is in the 65 ter summary, please supply subsequent summaries to cover the topics you intend to cover, and I think that must close the point at that point. Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Licina. We have quite a lot of ground to cover so I would ask to you follow the same practice; if you could just listen closely to my question and focus your answers on my questions. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You remember yesterday you spoke about the HDZ as a Croatcentric and Serbophobic party. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't saying that only about the HDZ but also about the other Croatian parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me focus just for a moment on the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If I could see on the e-court, please, a document which -- I believe we've managed to get all the documents in e-court thanks to a lot of hard work on the part of Ms. Walpita, which I appreciate very much. I hope it's there. The ERN in B/C/S is 00440884 to 0809, I believe. The English translation is 03017013 to 7055. And I think because it's a fairly lengthy document, if with the assistance of the usher I could give a B/C/S copy to the witness, it might make this go quicker. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, while we wait for this to come up on our screen, this is material relating to the first general assembly of the HDZ in Zagreb in 1990. That's right -- isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what it says on the cover page. That's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'd like you to look in particular, if you'll turn to -- you'll see it's page number 22 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's on page 17 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, here is where appears the Statute of the Croatian Democratic Union. Do you find that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could just flip to Article 10, please. It's actually Article 10.2. This is one of the reasons for and principles of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm just looking at the e-court screen. This should be on page 23 at the bottom, it shows of the B/C/S, just so we could get on to the right page, but I believe you have it before you. There it says that one of the reasons and principles of the HDZ is to further the transformation of the Republic of Croatia into a democratic parliamentary multi-party state that shall guarantee and ensure all the basic rights and liberties of every citizen, irrespective of the race or nationality or religious persuasion, political views and belief, of gender or of status of that person. That's what it says there; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Article 10.2 that's what it says. However, in 10.1 it says that they are going to strive for securing the right of the Croatian people for self-determination and to establish the independent state. So these two articles actually rule each other out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, there is nothing in this document that says that that's the case, is there? It doesn't say that 10.1 rules out 10.2. That doesn't make any sense, does it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It makes sense because Croatia, up until then, was a state of two constitutive peoples and by that very fact, if 10.1 were to be implemented, thereby the rights of Serbs would be cancelled out. So 10.2, then, would be brought into question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, we'll talk about that more later but there is nothing in Article 10 here that you see that is Serbophobic, is there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- you can interpret this item clearly that there is Croatocentrism, the placing of the Croatian people in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: We might look at it later but the Statute of the SDS also specifically mentions the Serbian people; isn't that right? Is the SDS a Serbocentric party, according to your view?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, because in the SDS statute, the rights of the Croatian people are never disputed. We did not dispute the right of the Croatian people to self-determination, but we also wanted to have the right to self-determination for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And that's exactly the same as -- it's very similar in 10.2 where it says that will guarantee and ensure all the basic rights and liberties of every citizen. It says that right there, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm going back to 10.1 again, where the secession of Croatia is being sought, and the secession of Croatia could not be carried out without the agreement of the Serbian people. The Serbian people did not agree to the secession of Croatia. The two people needed to reach accord on that, and that is why, in this approach, the rights of one party were being disputed or violated or suppressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You equate the HDZ emphasis or the support of Croatian independence as Serbophobic. Those things, to you, are the same thing, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
