utterances.text: I spoke about Serbophobia of the HDZ when I spoke about the pre-election campaign, in that context, the messages sent by the HDZ in the pre-election campaign were definitely Serbophobic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let's move on in this document a little bit. Please look at Article 15.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the statute?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Just a few Articles down from where you were just looking. There it says that -- essentially I'll paraphrase because the grammar is odd. It says the HDZ may join as members all persons of age who agree with the HDZ programme, principles and statute. There is nothing there that says you had to be a Croat to join the HDZ or that Serbs couldn't participate in HDZ. Nothing to that effect, is there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I didn't dispute that at all, so I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please go further on in the document. Actually, after the end of the Statute. And there is a message to the citizens of Croatia and to the entire Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I believe it's page 39 in the B/C/S version. It's page 34 in the English translation. Do you find that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The election declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. That was my next question. This actually -- this is an announcement specifically referencing those elections that you just mentioned, correct? It says that in the first line.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And then further down the page, it says, "Voting for the HDZ, you are voting for," and then it gives a number of bulleted points. I want you to look at number 4. This says, doesn't it, that voting for the HDZ is a vote for transformation of Croatia into a democratic multi-party, parliamentary state based on the observance of human rights and liberties of all its citizens. That's what it says, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Number 6 it says a vote for the HDZ is for the full and real equality of all citizens of the Republic of Croatia, irrespective of their nationality - Croatian, Serbian, Italian, Jewish or other - for equal rights of the Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Islamic, and any other religion and of all the ideological persuasions. It says that, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm not discussing any manifestos or official documents. I spoke about what was taking place during the pre-election campaign. I spoke about the statements of the HDZ officials, and I spoke about their pre-election campaign. This is what I was describing when I said that that was Serbophobic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And in this declaration, which was part of the pre-election campaign, there is nothing Serbophobic there, is there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a relative issue, what you're saying. There is nothing Serbophobic in the meetings. For example, there was a meeting between Tudjman and Raskovic. But you can't pull things out of context in order to create the whole picture and you need the whole picture in order to assess the work of a political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me turn you to another subject. Also yesterday you mentioned a few statements, or alleged statements, by Stjepan Mesic. One about, "All Serbs would be able to fit under one umbrella." Do you remember saying that? Do you remember attributing that statement to Stjepan Mesic? That's at transcript 33 and 34, if that's of assistance to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember, I can't be fully precise about it but that statement was given either in Brinj or in Gospic. At any rate, in Lika. And that was the statement that I quoted and that was the meaning of it, that all Serbs would fit either under one umbrella or under one plum tree. That was the essence of it, and it was mentioned in various meetings and gatherings. I just quoted that one example.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you ever hear him state these words? You've now given two different versions of what he just said but did you ever actually hear this statement?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm mentioning two different versions but the meaning is the same. When I say fit under one plum tree, that means just that, that there would be so many of them that they would be able to fit under one tree, or under one umbrella. I heard that because that was reported in the media. It was widely known. As I said to you, one could witness such atmosphere. I myself was living in Zagreb at the time and I attended many party gatherings back in 1989 and 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: My question was did you hear or see Stjepan Mesic say those words, this statement that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, this statement was broadcast on television. There were excerpts from the speech on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you sure or are you just guessing? Do you remember seeing and hearing this speech?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I remember, yes. I'm quite sure of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, the reason I ask that is because he never said that. He never made the statement. Stjepan Mesic never said those words, did he?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't put in my mouth something that I didn't say. So don't say, did he? I was called here to come and tell the truth, to tell about what I heard and what I saw. And this is what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The answer is simple, Mr. Licina. Did Mr. Stjepan make that statement? That is the "did he" at the end of the question is neither here nor there. Just answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this took place some 15 years ago, as far as I can remember, my answer is yes. This was in 1990 in the pre-election campaign. I'm not sure about the place, whether it was Gospic or Brinj, but it was one of these two towns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And did you actually witness it, that is see it on television, or did you hear it specifically of your own --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw it on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, there was another statement which you attribute to Stjepan Mesic. You said on page 34 of the transcript yesterday that his second statement was to the effect that the Serbs could only take with them as much soil as would be stuck to their shoes. Do you remember testifying about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember what his precise words were or do you have different versions of this statement as well?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only difference in two versions has to do with the specific name of the footwear. He said "opanci," and the meaning of it was derogatory because this is the type of footwear normally worn by farmers or peasants, and this was yet another insult addressed to Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You say the only difference is two versions, so are you saying that you also heard two versions of this statement?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not that I heard of two versions. I heard only of one and the word used was "opanci," referring to the footwear. It wasn't shoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you actually -- you saw and heard Stjepan Mesic, be it on television or in person, I'm not concerned about that, but you saw or heard him say those words, this statement you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Because in fact Mr. Mesic has explained to this Tribunal that what he in fact said was that Serbs did not transform Croatia into Serbia just by bringing Serb land on their shoes. That's something very different, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Stjepan Mesic said precisely what I told you, that the Serbs could take only as much soil as could be stuck on their shoes, "opanci," and that meant that the Serbs had come to Croatia from elsewhere, which is not true, because the Serbs had always lived there in the territory of Croatia. They hadn't arrived there from some place else, even though that was the impression that they tried to create, because they wanted to convey to the world that these were aggressors who had come from elsewhere. As far back as I can remember, all my ancestors had always lived there, and the same applies to all of my friends. This statement, however, was meant to create an impression that these people were the aggressors who needed to be expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me turn to another subject now. It's one that you raised earlier and it's this difference between a constituent nation and a minority. Do you remember Her Honour Judge Nosworthy asked you a question about this yesterday. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And at page 71 of the transcript yesterday, you gave this explanation. You said, "Had they -" meaning the Serbs - "been a minority, then the situation would have been different. Then they would have not had all the rights, and there could have been a secession without approval of the Serbs. However, if Serbs are a constituent nation, then their consent is required for secession because a nation -- because a nation comes before a public -- republic. That is the essence of that." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that it is a nation, not a republic, that has a right to sovereignty, and it was the Serbs and Croats who were two constituent nations who were entitled to sovereignty. If they lost the status of constituent nation, then the situation would be different and the Serbs would no longer have the right to decide about their fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, that's the only consequence of this change in the constitution, right? The only consequence of making Serbs a minority is that you lose the right to veto secession, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the mother of all issues, and this is the essence of the conflict, both the political and, as it later turned out, the military one. So this could not be reduced to a minor issue. This is the key issue in this entire process.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Under both the Yugoslav and the Croatian constitutions, minorities enjoyed protection of all basic human rights; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not discussing human rights here. I'm discussing national rights. The national right of Serbs was threatened, and also their human rights were at risk. After losing their national rights, they lost their human rights as well. We had bad memories from World War II. Thus our reaction was quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In a second I'll get into the connection between World War II and the 1990s according to you, but you do accept that the Serbs constituted a numerical minority in Croatia, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that before the Second World War, Serbs constituted 37 per cent of the population of Banovina Croatia. It was the genocide that reduced their percentage to 12 per cent after the war. Also, some Serbs declared themselves later as Yugoslav, thus further reducing the percentage of Serbs by three times. Thus, it was logical for Serbs to defend their status as a constituent nation because they had a very bitter experience from World War II. As to what had happened to them, when they were reduced down to a minority, it was an open season on Serbs. Over 1 million of Serbs were killed during World War II in various Ustasha camps. They were buried in pits and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, you're quite far from my question. You accept, do you not, that Serbs constituted a numerical minority in Croatia. Whether it's 37 per cent or 12 per cent, in terms of numbers, Serbs were a minority; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs were not a minority. They were a constituent people. Therefore, I will not accept that the Serbs were a minority. Similarly, I do not wish to say that Croats were a minority either. None of us were a minority. Once you reduce the status of a nation down to a minority, then there is a constitutional meaning to it and just discussing figures doesn't mean much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, putting aside the constitutional meaning and just discussing figures, do you not accept that the Serbs constituted numerically a minority in Croatia? Just answer that question.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was questionable too. There is data produced by Professor Slobodan Komazica who wrote an academic paper on this about the reduction of the number of Serbs in Croatia from long time ago. So that is questionable too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Now about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Is the professor contending that there were more Serbs than Croatians, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: -- the majority, because the simple question that has just been asked is do you accept the fact that there were fewer Serbs, that they were lesser in number? And to me, I do not see why you're procrastinating. Please go to the question directly and answer it once and for all. You have to confront it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number of Serbs in Croatia was reduced by means of genocide during World War II, and the result of the genocide can never be accepted. Therefore, I cannot discuss it in those terms. I can only tell you about the figures in the formal sense. There were 12 per cent of Serbs out of the total population in Croatia. So, yes, that is the figure, but the Serbs were a nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, this is one of the ongoing themes of the SDS not only in 1990s but today, that whenever you're asked questions about Croatia in the 1990s you constantly try to turn the focus back to World War II. Isn't that a theme that was used repeatedly by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Black, we have bitter memories. Great victims, great losses, and, yes, this issue is very close to our heart. There isn't a single family who didn't lose somebody in World War II, so we have to pay tribute to those victims. We cannot forget that, just like the Jews always mention their victims in World War II, the Serbs have an equal right to mention their victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No one disputes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: One moment please. Mr. Licina, Mr. Black, I'm sorry to interrupt you. I do wish to consult the Presiding Judge and the other judge in a matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, and Mr. Black, if you will, I have consulted with the learned Presiding Judge and the other judge, Judge Hoepfel, and the record should show that in respect of the question put by Mr. Black, as to the numbers of Serbs and whether they were in a minority at the relevant time, the record should disclose that the witness refuses to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I'll proceed to the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's just interrupt you once and for all. Can I just ask a question to the witness. Mr. Licina, at page 52, paragraph 2 of the transcript today, you said, "Thus it was logical for Serbs to defend their status as a constituent nation because they had a very bitter experience from World War II," and you continued to carry on in that theme. My question to you is: Did the Serbs do what they did during 1991 to 1995 because of their bitter experience in World War II? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbs didn't do anything bad in this war. The Serbs simply defended themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. My question to you is, and I'll ask you it again: Did the Serbs do what they did during 1991 to 1995 because of their bitter experience during World War II? Is that how you explain the conduct of the Serbs during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, the Albanians in Kosovo, for example, were a minority and they were never given nationhood status. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, but Albanians could not have been given the status of a nation because they have their own mother state, Albania. In the former Yugoslavia, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, it was the Slovenes, Croats, Serbs, Macedonians, and Muslims and Montenegrins who were the constituent nations, according to the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But with the break-up of Yugoslavia, the Croatian -- the Croatian Serbs and the Krajina Serbs in particular, they have their own motherland, too; Serbia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. That's not true because the Serbs in Croatia were a constituent nation. The Serbs were a constituent nation at the level of the entire Yugoslavia. It was Yugoslavia that was our state.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But with the break-up of Yugoslavia, and the secession of Croatia, then it makes sense, doesn't it, that the Serbs would be a minority because they had their motherland in Serbia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That doesn't make sense because the Serbs were a constituent people in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well. They had the right to sovereignty, which was guaranteed to them by all constitutions from the Second World War to 1990. Finally, in World War II, the Serbs, up until 1944, constituted 90 per cent of the anti-fascist forces in Croatia -- rather, in Yugoslavia. And the same applied in Croatia. As a result of which the Serbs were granted the status of a constituent nation, both in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were entitled to sovereignty in the territory of all of these republics within Yugoslavia. Serbia cannot be a mother state of Serbs from Krajina because we had not come there from Serbia. No; we had lived there always.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, that's not the test, when you came there, because you don't dispute that the Albanians had lived in Kosovo for all that time, or do you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did, but they were a national minority. They had their state; Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just one more question and I'm going to move away from this topic. The Serbs were allowed to vote in the referendum on Croatian independence, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs were banned from organising their own referendum back in 1990, so it's quite cynical to say that the Serbs were allowed to have a referendum within Croatia. They attempted to prevent, to block, the Serbs from expressing their will in August, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Again I'm going to ask you first to focus on my question. Serbs were allowed to vote in the referendum on Croatian independence, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, you didn't answer it. They were allowed to vote in the referendum on Croatian independence, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs, as a constituent nation, scheduled a referendum in August, and this is something that the state of Croatia tried to prevent. So it wasn't acceptable for the Serbs to vote in a referendum where numerically they would have been outvoted. Thus, it is quite cynical to claim that the Serbs were allowed to vote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, were the Serbs allowed to vote in the Croatian referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The referendum on Croatian independence wasn't organised in the entire territory of the then Croatia. Thus, only some of the Serbs, only part of the Serbs, were able to vote in the formal, legal sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, I'm not asking you whether the Serbs were able to vote. I'm asking you were the Serbs allowed to vote in the referendum, the Croatian referendum on independence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Formally, yes, but practically no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, were the Serbs allowed to vote in the Croatian independence referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already answered this question. The Serbs as a nation were prevented from expressing their will. Serbs as citizens would have been outvoted because of their numbers. The Serbs did not go and vote at that referendum although formally they were allowed to go and vote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, I'll ask you for the very last time. Were the Serbs allowed to vote in the Croatian referendum on independence? The answer to that question is either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Formally, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The -- will the record show that you have once again refused to answer the question. I think this may be a convenient time to take a break. We come back at half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, let me go to one aspect of what you said yesterday that relates to these amendments to the Croatian constitution and see if I understood you correctly. I believe you said that the amendments to the Croatian constitution were adopted in July, 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And then you suggested that the Serbs reacted to that by creating the Association of Municipalities of Northern Dalmatia and Lika; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Association of Municipalities was formed by the Serbs in June, whereas the reaction to the amendments to the constitution was reflected politically in the Serb Assembly or the Serb gathering in Srb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for that clarification. The real purpose, then, of creating the Association of Municipalities of Northern Dalmatia and Lika, that was a move toward ethnic separation by the Serbs even before these amendments to the constitution; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not correct. The Association of Municipalities was an Association of Municipalities with interests in common, and that was not the significance. The municipalities that formed the association are three adjoining municipalities, and they had much in common, in any case. There was already a blockade by the central republican government, and it was quite logical for these municipalities to form an economic association.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, looking at your answer, you seem to give two different responses. You say, no, it wasn't about ethnic separation, but then you say that there had been a blockade by the central republican government and it was logical for them to form an association. So I don't understand what you're saying. Was this a response to Croatian activities or was this a move by the Serbs on their own, seeking ethnic separation in June of 1990?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb Democratic Party proclaimed its political goals, advocating different degrees of Serb autonomy. The first degree was cultural autonomy. This implied associations of municipalities. For your information, most of the municipalities inhabited by Serbs were considered less developed municipalities. That's how they were treated in the then Croatia. And so logically they were oriented toward one another. They had been neglected by the Republic of Croatia and it had a cultural and economic significance for these municipalities to associate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And these municipalities were Knin, Benkovac, Gracac, Donji Lapac, Obrovac, and Titova Korenica; that's right, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first it was Knin, Gracac, and Donji Lapac, and the others that you mentioned joined later on. These were also territorially adjacent municipalities so that together they formed a territorial whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And by June of 1990, all of those municipalities that I mentioned were part of the Association of Municipalities, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not correct. The decision to establish the Association of Municipalities took place at the end of June, and the Association of Municipalities of Northern Dalmatia and Lika was established by the three municipalities which associated in late June. The other municipalities joined later on, during the summer and autumn, and I can't recall the precise dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could we see Exhibit 140 on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It should appear on the screen in front of you in just a moment, Mr. Licina. If we could just zoom in slightly on the top half of that document, please. Mr. Licina, looking at the screen in front of you, you recognise this, don't you, as the decision on the establishment of the association of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And it's dated the 27th of June, 1990. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, the end of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could scroll down, please, so we can see all of Article 1. Right there is good. The second paragraph of Article 1, Mr. Licina, says that the regional Association of Municipalities of Northern Dalmatia and Lika includes the municipalities of Knin, Benkovac, Gracac, Donji Lapac, Obrovac, and Titova Korenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But for this decision to be valid, it had to be confirmed by each individual municipality. What I'm saying is that Knin, Gracac, and Donji Lapac were the first three municipalities to issue this decision, and the others then approved the decision later on. I'm not denying that they were all members of the association, but the association was fully formed only once each particular municipality had issued this decision. They had to verify the decision. Each individual local assembly had to verify the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that it was ratified later by the municipalities but in fact the decision, as we saw, was on the 27th of June, 1990, for all of these municipalities to form part of the Association of Municipalities; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but I repeat: The decision entered into force when the first three municipalities ratified it, whereas the others joined later on, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, I think you've said that. I'm sorry for interrupting you, but we need to focus and there is no need to repeat things which you've already testified about. All of these municipalities later joined the SAO Krajina and then the RSK; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These municipalities formed the SAO Krajina. They didn't join it. The assembly of the Association of Municipalities transformed this into the SAO Krajina. They were the founders of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And they later, all of these municipalities, pertained to the RSK. Isn't that also correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these municipalities, as the SAO Krajina, actually were united with the Serb district of Western Slavonia, Baranja and Srem and the other Serb district so that these three the regions together formed the Republic of Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In other words, your answer is yes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please, again, just focus on my questions and give an answer that's complete but concise. Please try to do that. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am giving you concise replies but I have to explain. When you say "joined," they didn't join it, they formed it. I had to give you an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Again I'll put it to you, sir, the real purpose of this Association of Municipalities was taking a first step towards a separate Serb state; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: First, they had the Association of Municipalities, then the SAO Krajina, and then the RSK. Those were all logical steps towards a separate Serb state; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political moves of the Serbs in the Krajina were conditioned by the political moves of Croatia. We only carried out political moves by which we protected our rights. Therefore I see no logic in what you're saying. The fact that these municipalities were part of this doesn't mean anything. I'm speaking of the political concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask you about a different political move, let's say. On the 18th of July, 1990, you and Vojislav Lukic, President of the SDS municipal board, went to the Gracac Public Security Services, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. Vojislav Lukic was the president -- was not the president of the municipality, and it was the 17th of August, 1990. I was the president of the municipal board of the SDS and a deputy in the assembly, and Vojislav Lukic was the president of the municipality. And this was in the night between the 17th and the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You're quite right. Thank you for correcting me about the position of Mr. Lukic. But you did in fact go to the Gracac police station on that date?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could see on the e-court, please, a document with the ERN 02663436A. It's the bottom half of a newspaper that's been photocopied. The English translation is ET 02663436 to 3436A. If we could please see that on the screen. Thank you. If we could focus in on, I believe it's the second column at the bottom there of what's seen on the screen. Yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, I don't know if you can read that. Let me read to you what it says and you can follow along and tell me if it's correct. It says that you and Mr. Lukic and Dr. Gacesa [phoen] visited the Gracac SJS to make the employees of that station sign the statement dated the 1st of October saying that they would not obey the orders of the Republic of Croatia Ministry of Interior since they are, in their opinion, aimed against the Serbian people and the inhabitants of Gracac. And that's correct, isn't it, that you went there in order to make the policemen sign a statement that they would disobey the orders of the Croatian Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not correct. As far as I can see, this is an excerpt from the Croatian newspaper called Vjesnik. As I said during the examination-in-chief, on that day I arrived from Zagreb, I went from Korenica to Gospic, and this was in the late evening, and when I was there with Vojislav Lukic, Mr. Gacesa was not present, and we were in the public security station because the then minister of the interior, Josip Boljkovac, was asking for talks through a special police line, which is why we went to the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: One technical issue. I don't know if Your Honours are able to find the translation. We got it very late, so it's possible it's not on e-court. I apologise. We will get it into e-court as soon as it's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Black, an additional question is the date of this Article. On the e-court system it's dated with 18 of July and the witness corrected your question by speaking of August. Could we clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember the date of this visit to the Gracac police station?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember very well. This was the 17th of August, two days before our referendum of the 19th of August. Therefore I'm sure that it was the 17th of August, not July. As far as I can see, this is from a newspaper, so probably there is a mistake there. I am quite certain that this was the 17th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You were not in the Gracac police station in July; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to the 17th of August, I was in Zagreb. On the 17th of August, I travelled from Zagreb. I had had some party duties to perform in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid at this point I can't, independently of what the witness says, verify the date of the article. I will get that done and report back tomorrow. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, I put to you that this incident did in fact happen, that you did ask the policemen in Gracac to disobey the orders of the Croatian minister of the interior. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the course of the day, or rather, the evening before, in the night between the 16th and the 17th, weapons had been taken from the Gracac police station and the citizens, as a result, were very disturbed. There was a gathering -- I'm telling you now what I learned later on from my fellow party members, because I wasn't there. I arrived in Gracac in the evening of the 17th. It was about 10 p.m. So I wasn't there during the day but only in the evening. After that, I went to the municipality and I think that this conversation with Boljkovac took place after midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If you weren't there, I won't take it any further at this point. Let me ask you now about the Serb Assembly in Srb on the 25th of July, 1990, which you've mentioned. It's correct that that assembly was attended by some 100.000 Croatian Serbs; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that assembly, there were 100.000 Serbs from Croatia, not Croatian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the assembly passed a declaration on the sovereignty and autonomy of the Serbian people, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The assembly in Srb issued a declaration on the sovereignty and autonomy of the Serb people and formed the Serb National Council as its executive organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you yourself were present at this assembly, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there personally and I was elected to the Serb National Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could see Exhibit 141 on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, you recognise this, don't you, as the declaration on the sovereignty and autonomy of the Serbian people adopted at that assembly on the 25th of July, 1990?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And in paragraph 1 there, it says the Serbian nation is, in accordance with its geographic, historical, social and cultural characteristics, a sovereign nation with all the rights entailed in the sovereignty of a nation. And then in the second paragraph, right below that, still in number 1, it says, "The Serbian nation in the SR Croatia is fully entitled to opt for a federate --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the reply.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you scroll it up a little bit. A little more, a little more.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Licina, for pointing that out. I'll start again on the second paragraph. You'll see there that it says: "The Serbian nation in SR Croatia is fully entitled to opt for a federate or confederate system of state government, either jointly with the Croatian nation or independently." That's what it says, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And those are references towards not just Serb sovereignty but the possibility of Serb independence, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb people proclaimed its desire to remain in the common state. Therefore, the Serb people does not deny the Croatian people the right to have a state, but on the other hand, they demand the same right for themselves. They only want the same right that the Croatian people have; nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you're demanding the right to have a separate Serb state. That's what you're saying here in this declaration. You and the other people present at this assembly in July of 1990.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We are asking for Croatia to remain in the common federal state, in which case we advocate cultural autonomy for the Serbs. However, if the character of the federal state is changed, we want the next degree of rights, depending on whether it's confederation or secession.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you seem to be talking around the answer but what you just said, this includes the idea of secession, of Serb secession from Croatia, right? That's what is at issue in this declaration as one of the options on the table.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. For the Serbs to secede, it's first necessary for the Croats to secede from the joint state. We didn't want any kind of secession, either the one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In fact, you did want secession, didn't you? The Serb leadership already in July, 1990, was looking towards the time that they could have a Serb state separate from Croatia. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. That's not correct. Let me go back to the key point. The Serb nation is a constituent nation in Croatia and has the same rights as the Croatian people. We do not deny anything to the Croatian people but, by the same token, we don't want any of our rights to be taken away from us. All our political moves were conditioned by the political moves of the leadership of the Republic of Croatia. You cannot look at it outside the overall context. You have to see the whole picture to reach certain conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. I have been refraining up to this point from putting it forward. The Prosecutor has the right in cross-examination to put leading questions, but he doesn't have the right to disinform the witness. Let him put the whole document to the witness. Underneath Article 1 there is Article 2, which says that the Serb people have the right to autonomy. In spite of Article 2, which is only two lines below, the Prosecutor is pressuring the witness and leading him to an erroneous conclusion. The document has already been presented to the Chamber and the witness has spoken very precisely about this document, particularly about the autonomy. Of course, the Prosecutor does have the right to press the witness, but not to deny the witness the entire text of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour, briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: First of all, this seems like an issue for re-examination. It doesn't really seem to be an objection. But -- and that's my response, Your Honour. And I'm happy to talk about Article 2 of this document, if I may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, Defence counsel has asked that we look at Article 2 of this same document.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we scroll up -- down. Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is there anything here in this document that gives the explanation that you have just given about how you don't take any rights away from the Croats, you just want the same rights that they have been given, or they assert for themselves?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a full explanation here, in fact. I can read it out. It says, based on its sovereignty, the Croatian people in Croatia have a right to autonomy. The content of that autonomy will depend on whether Yugoslavia is organised as a federal or confederal state. The content of the autonomy will depend on whether the order of Yugoslavia is federal or confederal. In conditions of a federal state, the Serb people have a right to use the Serb language, the Cyrillic alphabet, school curricula, and so on. So this is purely cultural autonomy, nothing else, in case there is a federation. And there is a very clear explanation of what I said previously, that all our moves were conditioned by the moves of the Croatian state leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It doesn't say that anywhere in here, does it, that the Serb moves were conditioned by the Croatian moves. That doesn't appear in Article 2 or anywhere else in this document, as I see it.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears in Article 2, in paragraph 1, in the second sentence, where it says the content of the autonomy would depend on the federal or confederal order of the future Yugoslavia. So it does depend on that, and this is very clearly stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I'd like to show something on the Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please let me first ask something to this declaration. Mr. Licina, did this proclamation express in any way what you first said, that your desire to remain in the common state? Was this expressed here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, it was expressed just by the fact that the political position of the Serbs was defined; what their position was on autonomy, how they would relate to the future order, both of Croatia and the future order of the federal state. So all of that is expressed. This sentence explains it all, that it would depend on -- the content of the autonomy would depend on the federal or confederative order of Yugoslavia. So that would be item 2, the first paragraph, the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I can't really see in this sentence an expression of the Serb desire to remain in a common state. Or can you help me finding that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Reflected in the aspiration of the Serbs for a federal order, the Serbs were not asking for anything more than cultural autonomy if the state should remain a federal one. I think that that is what it says as the paragraph continues. Actually item 2, paragraph 2, conditions of the federal state order. The Serb people then declare what they would need to have in the event of a federal order or a confederal one. Since the state at the time was still a federal one, this is then what we were in favour of, as it is stated here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please help me. I still don't understand you, because if you read further on in the paragraph 4 of this Article 2, it speaks of the other option of the confederate system, and is there any, if not desire, then at least preference expressed in this proclamation? Then you can show me that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then, when this declaration was drafted, the state was still a federal state formally. I don't see anything disputable in item 4, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness quotes from the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because in that case, the state would need to be recomposed. So then the Serbs, as part of the Croatian federal unit which defines its status as a confederal one, would also have to reformulate their own status within that state. It's quite logical. Because first of all, the Serbs were in favour of a federal order. Should such an order be changed, then it was logical that the Serbs would need to protect themselves, to raise the level of their status to a higher level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Witness, I didn't ask you for telling me what would be logical and what I would then have to conclude from your saying, but could you please answer my question. Is there any preference between the two options, federation or confederation, being expressed in this proclamation? And if yes, in which sentence, in which words do you find that expression of this desire or preference, at least? Please answer clearly and short.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a formal minority in terms of numbers, we had to be in a position to protect our national rights, so it was logical in that situation, or in that constellation of forces, for us to take the position that we did. Yes. It's clear, it's clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That was not what I asked you. Something about logic. But you -- first you said something about a desire to remain in the common state. Is this desire being reflected in the wording of this proclamation from Srb not? Yes or no. And if yes, then where, in which sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The declaration proclaims our position on what our position or the position of Serbs within Croatia should be. What the position of Serbs should be in Croatia if Croatia would remain a federal unit, and what the position would be if it became a confederal unit. We were in the position of adopting that in that particular form at that time. I do not see anything here that would indicate that we wished to secede from Croatia. Item 2 first cites the desire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Witness, please answer my question. I didn't ask you if there was anything expressed about a wish to secede but about a wish, about a desire, to remain in the common state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not explicitly stated in the text but the entire text is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That's enough. Thank you. Please, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. If we could watch a short video clip on the Sanction, please. And this is actually from Exhibit 497. It's an interview with Mr. Martic. As usual, I'm not sure which button we have to push. Could we broadcast the Sanction, please. Okay. It looks like the same e-court button as usual would get us the video. And if we could play that video now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we seem to have a technical problem. Have we changed to Sanction in the audiovisual booth? Is everything ready to go in there? I apologise, Your Honour, could I take 30 seconds to try to see if I can resolve this? I apologise, Your Honour. There seems to be an issue with our computer, so I'll skip it and come back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps I'll wait just a second to see if we have a resolution. I'll move on, Your Honour. I'm convinced now it's a problem with our computer here, not with the audiovisual or the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, sorry for that distraction. Because of that, I'm going to leave that topic now and maybe come back to it a little later. But let me ask you now about the 17th of August, 1990, the so-called log revolution. You remember that you suggested yesterday that Croatian actions on that day were intended to prevent the Serb referendum. I think you said that also today. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said the 17th of August, 1992, but it was actually 1990. Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It could have been a misstatement, but I do mean the 17th of August, 1990. And yesterday you testified that there were Croatian movements - I think you said you saw an APC - and that those movements were designed to prevent the Serb referendum. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 17th of August, I saw personally, because on that day I was travelling from Zagreb to Gracac, I saw in Korenica, which is about 70 kilometres from Gracac, I saw Croatian --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't need you to repeat what you said before. I just want to know if you remembered the topic, and you do remember the topic. But the Serbs actually did hold their referendum as scheduled, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So the Croatian operations did not prevent the Serb referendum.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian operations would probably have prevented the referendum had the army not reacted by having a plane of the JNA turn back a Croatian MUP helicopter that had set off in the direction of Benkovac, and had it not been for the Serb self-organising and the barricades, there probably would have been an incursion into the Serb municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The Croatian government activity on that day, it was -- had nothing to do with the referendum, did it? It was about taking control of weapons, weapons that it perceived as being threatened by the Krajina Serbs; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not right. There were two processes at that time. One of them was the forming of new police stations that I talked about in places where there was a Croatian population, but which were within municipalities where the Serbs had local power and local parliaments. At the same time, there was a confiscation of weapons from the police reserve forces and from the police stations in the centres of those municipalities; Benkovac, Obrovac, Gracac, and the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the forming of new police stations has to do with this, but the Croatian operations on that day were about seizing weapons from police reserve forces because they thought that the Krajina Serbs wanted control of those weapons; isn't that right? That's what the Croatian operations were about on the 17th of August, 1990. Nothing to do with the referendum.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What you have said is not correct. I am going back again to the following. There should be a complete picture. At the same time, new police stations were formed. Until that time, police -- we are talking about places where there were no police stations and there was no need for these police stations to exist. Then also the police stations that already existed were being disbanded and weapons were being confiscated from those police stations. This was happening on the eve of the referendum. So when you put those two things together, then you can see what was actually going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: About the new police stations, you know, yesterday you mentioned these a couple of times and you said they were illegal, but these were Croatian police stations on Croatian territory. They were perfectly legitimate, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not perfectly legitimate because those police stations were formed only in Serb municipalities. There were no new police stations being formed, for example, in the municipality of Varazdin, for example, and in some village within the municipality of Varazdin. There was no police station being formed in the municipality of Cakovec, but new police stations were being formed in Serbian communities and that is how they had that political context.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the reason they were being formed in these Serbian municipalities was, number 1, to protect the Croat population, and 2, as a response to the Serb organising that we've been talking about. That's why those new police stations were formed and that's why they were justified. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct, because there were no threats coming from the Serbs. There were no killings. I mentioned earlier during the examination-in-chief that until the Sveti Rok barracks was de-blockaded, up until that time, five citizens of the Gracac municipality were killed. Therefore, they were those who were generating the crisis. There were no attacks on our part. At the same time, there was an attempt to prevent the legally elected municipal organs from having free passage in that area. They were not able to move around freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me turn to another thing that you said about the 17th of August, 1990. Is it your position that these barricades were erected at the same time through so many parts of Serbian Krajina, and this was all spontaneous, without any organisation? Is that your position? Because that's what you've suggested yesterday and today.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a spontaneous thing, and in order to illustrate that the barricades did go up spontaneously, we actually had a problem to communicate amongst the municipalities. There was -- it was not easy to communicate between the municipalities of Gracac and Knin. So the people erected those barricades spontaneously. If you were travelling from Gracac to Knin, you would come across four or five such barricades that the people put up. This happened in other places as well. Had there been any organisations, then the barricades would have been only on the outlying areas of those territories, but they were not. Actually, they cropped up all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood you. Are you suggesting that the barricades were erected to improve communications or that they were a barrier to communications? I just didn't understand your response.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barricades were erected on self initiative and because of the fear of the people. Before I said that the Serbian people had strong and painful historical memories and it just reacted in a logical way. It was also an impulsive reaction in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You know, don't you, that Petar Gracanin, the Serbian minister of the interior, later publicly took credit, let's say, for suggesting the idea of putting up barricades at this time. You're aware of those statements?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, an objection. Mr. Gracanin, Petar Gracanin was a general. He was not the Serbian minister of internal affairs. He was the federal secretary for internal affairs. He was the minister of the interior of the state of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I accept the correction, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. But so it was not an objection, it was a correction, Mr. Milovancevic, was it? You may proceed, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I apologise for the misstatement there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But you're aware of those statements where he said he had taken credit, or he said he had suggested these barricades be erected? You're familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There were many statements but these were made by politicians who at a certain political moment want to make themselves seem important. But I'm not aware of any, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that politicians with certain political motives can't be reliable, can't be trusted? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not suggesting that, but no one can be said to have given an exact statement every single time. I can't say that I have heard it. It's a question of perhaps when he said it. As far as I know, he had nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But you do know that police, Serbian police, manned many of the barricades. You accept that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. I don't know what Serbian police my learned friend from the Prosecution is talking about. This is a territory of the Republic of Croatia, a federal unit within Yugoslavia. All the police on Croatian territory belong to the Ministry of the Internal Affairs of Croatia. There was no Serbian police on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. When there were some problems, then they would manifest in areas that were with a majority Serb or a majority Croat population. This naming of the police in such a way is quite contrary to the actual and official names of those police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I withdraw the question, and may I rephrase it, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You do know, Mr. Licina, that police of Serb ethnicity manned many of the barricades on August 17th of 1990. You know that, don't you? That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of something of the sort. I know that the barricades were a result of self-organising. If there were some policemen present, then they were present there in their capacity as local residents. They had not come from somewhere else. I can't affirm that there was a policeman at every barricade, but I can tell you that there was no pre-organising involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You know about the defence staff that was formed on the 17th of August, 1990, to organise these barricades and other activity. You've heard of that defence staff which later became the Council for National Resistance, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could have that on e-court please. The ERN is 02163347 to 3352. If we could just briefly see the last page of this document, please. Thank you. If we could scroll down to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, you recognise the name on the left there, Zdravko Tolimir, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And he was in fact the head of the JNA security organs at sometime, maybe not in September of 1990, but he was part of the JNA security organs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Zdravko Tolimir was one of the officers in the Knin Corps. That's all I can tell you about him. Back in 1991. I don't know about 1990. And I don't know -- or rather, I think that he went to Bosnia after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And just for clarity, when you say of the Knin Corps, that's the Knin Corps of the JNA, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Knin Corps of the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA. I remember that he was one of the officers. I don't know him personally, I'm familiar with his name, and I think that later on he was in the army of Republika Srpska, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's sufficient. Thank you. Just before we move away from the last page, it basically says here that he took this statement, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thanks. Now if we could look at the first page again of this statement, and if we scroll down a bit, the person giving the statement says that he was an employee of the Knin centre for informing. Do you see that there? The Knin informational centre, I guess that's what that means; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says there. Yes. That's what it should be based on what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And further down, it says -- it actually talks about him being at that centre on the evening of the 17th of August until the morning of the 18th of August, 1990. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This sentence, I remember these events well. Is that what you had in mind? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Exactly. If we could scroll down a little more, and next he goes on to say that he is aware that the staff for defence of Knin was formed, and then he says later on it was later renamed the Council of National Resistance. Does that spark your memory? Do you remember now about this Council for National Resistance that was formed on the 17th of August, 1990?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the staff. What I can see here is that this is a statement of a gentleman who is currently in Croatia. I think he's actually an official of a Croatian party. Maybe even in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This statement was given to the JNA, correct? It wasn't given to the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what it says here is correct, right, that there was a staff for defence of Knin created and it was later renamed the Council for National Resistance; and furthermore, it was headed by Milan Martic. This is all correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the statement of that gentleman. I can't confirm whether it's true or not. This is his statement. I know nothing about this so I can't confirm it either as accurate or not. Given his current political activities, I would take it with a grain of salt.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me just point you to a couple of other things and see if you know anything about these other statements. Maybe you don't. Further down, on page 3 of the English, which I believe is also page 3 of the B/C/S, if we could skip ahead to that page 3, it's that top paragraph there, I think, although I don't read B/C/S so it's a bit of a -- no, that's not -- it's the next paragraph down. Thank you. It says there that communication -- and this is talking about the 17th of August, 1990. It says communication is mainly with SDS activists and other people from municipalities who were engaged in self-organising of citizens for resistance in the event of an attack by MUP forces. In such a centralised system of operation, all information would be sent to Knin. Now, that's accurate, isn't it? You accept that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not accepting anything. This is just a statement given by a man. You are putting a statement to me, a statement that somebody gave to a JNA organ. The fact that he gave a statement doesn't carry a meaning. It doesn't mean that this is true. It just means that this is his statement. I cannot confirm it because I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you know nothing about the organisation that was going on in Knin, you know nothing about events in Knin or in Golubic on the 17th of August, 1990?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I would move this document into evidence, please. Could it be given a number and admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document will become Exhibit number 872.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: While I'm at it, Your Honour, I'm reminded that I neglected to ask for admission of the first document that we looked at, which is the HDZ document. It's the one that bears the ERN 00449884 to 9904, I believe. And the English translation starts at 03017013. I would ask that that document also be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May that document with that ERN number please be admitted into document -- into evidence and be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the HDZ general assembly material will become Exhibit 873.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, actually before we move away from this statement here taken by Tolimir, I just want to ask you a couple more things and see if you know about this because it's actually after the 17th of August, 1990. If we could turn to page 4 of the document, please. It's the bottom paragraph in B/C/S. It's about the middle of the page in English. Mr. Licina, here it says: "Concerning illegal arming of citizens, I can say that it is widespread. I know that about 1300 guns and 400 pistols have been infiltrated into the Knin and Obrovac municipalities. I know that 600 guns have arrived in Strmica. I think it was between the 15th of October, 1990, and the 19th of October, 1990." And then it says, "They came from a factory of RO Sport from Belgrade which runs a business in Knin." That's true, isn't it, that there was -- there were arms coming in from Serbia and other countries and being distributed to Serb -- citizens of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of anything of the sort. The weapons that were present at the barricades were personal weapons of the people there; hunting rifles. Some people were just armed with stones. I can't comment this. This is a statement provided by somebody to a military organ, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just asking what you know based on some statements that are here, but I'm interested in what you know. If you look at the next page, page 5 -- actually, it's page 6 of the B/C/S. This statement also says that citizens were given weapons from the Knin SJS reservists, and it says those weapons were handed out on the 17th of August, 1990, after the Knin SJS warehouse was broken into. I know you said you weren't there, but you heard about that, didn't you? You heard about police reserve weapons being distributed to Serb citizens?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never said that I heard that the weapons had been distributed to Serb citizens. I don't remember ever stating something like that. I know that the weapons were --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. I'm not saying that you have stated this. I am saying you heard about that, didn't you? I'm asking you. Didn't you hear about weapons from the police station? And not just Knin's police station but other police stations, being distributed to Serb citizens?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: One other thing to see if you had heard of it, in the next paragraph down, there is a mention of Simo Dubajic [phoen] and Milan Martic handing out weapons. It says that people in town are openly talking about this. Did you -- did you hear about that, about Milan Martic participating in the distribution of weapons?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never heard of that. And as for Mr. Simo Dubajic, he was quite an interesting figure, but I have never heard anything of this sort, that it dates back to the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: On -- just so I'm clear -- Did you want to say something that dates back to the Second World War? It wasn't clear if we heard the entire interpretation there.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just about the name. Simo Dubajic was a well-known figure in the Second World War. He was one of the well-known Partizan commanders from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You think that's the same Simo Dubajic or a different one or you just don't know, it was just the name?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name sounds familiar. That's the only reference I have right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Just so I'm clear, you were not personally in Knin or Golubic on the 17th of August, 1990?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th of August, 1990, as I have said, I was in Zagreb up until 2 p.m., and then I set out to Gracac, arriving there in the late evening hours, maybe 10 p.m. So physically I was unable to be in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. I remember you actually testified about that before. Milan Babic was the president of the Knin municipality at that time, wasn't he, in August, 1990?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And president of the Serbian National Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: He was also on the main board of the SDS with you, and he was the president of the Association of Municipalities of Northern Dalmatia and Lika. Isn't that also correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Member of the main and executive board and president of the community of municipalities of Northern Dalmatia, Lika, and so on. He had a lot of posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Before I move away from the 17th of August, 1990, it's true, isn't it, that after that date, Milan Martic was viewed as a hero to the Serb people, based on his participation and his leadership in events on that day?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Martic, viewed in the context of all of his activities, was viewed as a hero in the Serbian Republic of Krajina. Over a number of years. But I can't link him to a specific date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you disagree with me that that really started on the 17th of August, 1990. That was really the first date of his emergence on to the scene as a Serb hero?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Milan Martic became known to the people after he gave a statement to the Croatian television to a journalist called Heni Erceg, I believe, when he said he wasn't going to put a chequerboard symbol on his cap. I think that that was his statement and this is how he became known to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember the date when Mr. Martic said that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was summertime of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we are at the end of the day. I'll have to continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we leave, in case this document gets off the screen by tomorrow, can I ask a question to the witness? Given your position that the barricades were a spontaneous activity by citizens in the Knin area and other areas, and in view of the position taken by the author of this statement, what comment, if any, do you have on the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't comment. Judging on the basis of this, this is a man who is currently in Croatia and politically active in a political party which represents itself as a Serbian party but in my view isn't. As for there being no organisation, this is confirmed by my earlier testimony. There were many barricades in our municipalities. Had this all been preorganised, it would have been done. These barricades would have been erected on the outlines of these municipalities, as the Prosecution is trying to portray, but these barricades were everywhere; between Lapac and Strbac, and they were cropping up everywhere, and this proves that they were spontaneous, because had it been preorganised, there would have been a system to it. This was random. I had to travel to Knin a lot in that period of time because a referendum was planned. And during those days, one would need about five hours to travel between Gracac and Knin, and this is a trip that normally takes one hour so we wouldn't be, on purpose, creating problems for our own travel. It's just not logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was the author of this statement in Croatia on the 2nd of December, 1990, when he made this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know him personally. His name appeared in the papers recently and I know that he's a president of a party in Croatia now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not the question that's put to you. You say you based your comment on the fact that this man is in Croatia, and I'm asking you when he made this statement, at the 2nd of December, 1990, was he in Croatia, if Croatia has anything to do with the content of his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the man. Therefore, I can't know whether he was there or wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you if you know the man. I'm asking you if the man was in Croatia on the 2nd of December, 1990. Please try to listen to the question and try to answer the question as succinctly and concisely and comprehensively as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very simply, I'm telling you I don't know. I don't know the man, so I can't know about his whereabouts. I simply don't know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why do you tell us then that he's in Croatia? You can't tell us about his whereabouts, but you've just told us that he's in Croatia and that's why you dispute his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I was saying is that he's in Croatia now and that he's active in politics there now. He's a chairman of a political party now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What has that got to do with a statement he made on the 2nd of December, 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I can just say that there is a political continuity there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then don't tell us irrelevancies if you don't know. Okay? Now, are you suggesting that if these barricades had been organised by somebody, they would not have appeared all over, as they did? They appeared all over because it was spontaneous? It seems to me to suggest the contrary to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it would be good if we could take a look at the map of that area and then I would be able to point out to you all the places where I know that barricades existed at the time, and then you would be able to see the illogical aspect of this claim. The barricades were erected between two Serb municipalities, say. Had there been a desire to organise this, and had it been planned in advance, we would not have tried to erect barricades between our own two municipalities. The barricades were erected basically next to all villages, which means that people rose up in protest in a spontaneous way. The mere location, placement of these barricades, illustrates the spontaneous nature of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you said that these barricades were all over and spontaneous, which demonstrated that therefore they were not organised. I'm trying to look at your text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everywhere within. Around and within. The barricades were everywhere, not only towards the outside world but only within the territory of Serbian municipalities. The barricades were erected even inside the Serbian territory, which made the traffic between two Serb localities difficult. Had there been a system preplanned, then these barricades would not have been erected and there were barricades erected between two Serb settlements which is an evidence of this being a spontaneous process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Let me in this context ask you a short question: In between a protest by whom? By local people of what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I used the word "protest." Maybe it was a mistranslation. It was a spontaneous process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Spontaneous process coming from whom; local Serbs or Croats or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A spontaneous process among the people in that territory. Mostly Serbs. But these barricades were erected throughout these Serbian municipalities. When one travelled from one Serbian municipality to another, one came across these barricades which were erected next to all villages. This shows the spontaneity of the process. It made our life difficult because we were in the process of organising the referendum and it was difficult for us to communicate, to travel between these settlements. The trip from Gracac to Knin, instead of 45 minutes, took five hours. Had we really organised all this in advance, we wouldn't have done it, because it was in our interest to conclude business as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm afraid, because of Judge Nosworthy's other commitments this afternoon, we will have to adjourn. We will have to resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning, the same courtroom. Hopefully we can continue with the same topic. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
